narration: We start with the INPUT block: the raw data the method consumes for a single indoor scene.
First input: the reconstructed 3D point cloud of the whole room.
Second input: the posed RGB frames of the same scene, captured as the camera moves through it.
Third input: the matching depth maps and camera poses, which link every pixel back to a 3D location.
Step one of the pipeline is 3D-aware two-D mask tracking, carried out inside this yellow block.
A superpoint is selected on the point cloud: a small cluster of points marking the object to segment.
The superpoint is projected into every camera, and a histogram of the projected points is built over the views.
The peak of the histogram gives the pivot view: the single frame in which the object is seen best.
The pivot view and the projected superpoint are handed to SAM two for segmentation.
SAM two returns a two-D mask of the object in the pivot view.
That mask, together with the 3D cues, seeds SAM two tracking across the rest of the video.
Tracking runs in both directions from the pivot frame: a backward pass and a forward pass over the sequence.
The result is a two-D mask track: a consistent mask for the object in every frame of the scene.
The mask track flows down into step two: 3D proposal refinement via mask optimisation.
The two-D mask track is first lifted back into 3D, giving a rough 3D mask candidate.
That candidate is then refined by an optimisation procedure, Algorithm one, which cleans up the 3D mask.
Optimisation yields the final 3D proposal for this object instance.
Repeating the whole process over all superpoints produces a class-agnostic 3D instance segmentation of the scene.
Finally, CLIP and a large language model label those instances, giving open-vocabulary and open-ended 3D instance segmentation: table, TV, desktop, monitor, and more.
